stories.title: Martin to address O'Connor sacking amid call for clarity
stories.summary: Taoiseach Micheál Martin is expected to address the sudden removal of HSE Chief Executive Anne O'Connor from her role in the Dáil today. Opposition politicians are demanding greater clarity on the sacking of Ms O'Connor but Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill insists the decision was exclusively a matter for members of the HSE board, whom she said are independent but have her support. The Government is expected to face sustained questioning on the developments in the Dáil during Leaders' Questions - with the Green Party calling for time to be set aside for a special Dáil debate. Members of the Dáil's Committee of Public Accounts and the Oireachtas Health Committee will also consider their next steps throughout the day - as they push for greater scrutiny of the events leading to Ms O'Connor's sacking. Last night, Mr Martin met Tánaiste Simon Harris, the leader of Independent TDs in Government Sean Canney and Ms Carroll MacNeill. He earlier met the Chief Executive of Cork University Hospital (CUH) Jennifer Kearney and other senior officials at the institution for several hours yesterday afternoon.

stories.title: Possible data breach at Dublin crèche software provider
stories.summary: A software provider for crèches and early education has said children's names, dates of birth and contact details of parents may have been exposed in what it called a "security incident". Little Vista, a Dublin-based childcare management software operator that describes itself as an "all-in-one" childcare management application, informed affected organisations of the breach, that it said resulted in unauthorised access to data. Staff and parents have been advised to be alert to unexpected contact as a result. However, exposure was limited "in many cases" the email said, meaning it may be data of just one individual at a service being accessed. Measures were put in place by Little Vista to secure the affected system and prevent further access, the email read, with no evidence found of the core database being accessed. As well as informing affected childcare providers, the company is understood to have reported the incident to the Data Protection Commission.

stories.title: Why do so many superstar CEOs turn out to be abusive managers?
stories.summary: Analysis: Many elite bosses are intelligent, motivated and passionate, but lack the capacity to understand employees who do not have the same traits Abusive supervisors regularly display hostile verbal or nonverbal behaviours towards the people who report to them, such as belittling subordinates or yelling at them. This style of management has beenwidely studied, and it is rarely seen as an effective way to manage organisations. It can work for a short while; employees who are yelled at or abused will often do what they are told. But, over time, abusive supervision often leads to stress, reduced satisfaction with and commitment to work and lower levels of performance. In recent years, there have been some spectacular reports of abusive supervision by high-flying CEOs. Jensen Huang was widely praised as CEO of Nvidia before being pushed out last week by the board of the company over reports of his sexual involvement with a suspected Chinese spy and with a high-level employee of Nvidia. He was then reinstated by the same board yesterday. During all of this, allegations of his abusive supervisory style are just starting to emerge. A story in the New York Times described a years-long pattern of Huang yelling at and humiliating executives, managers and executives at Nvidia. This story reports that he "told one executive that his mother should have aborted him, according to one witness. He said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them. And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and "pee on your brain." But Huang is not the only CEO accused of abusive supervision. There are numerous reports of Elon Musk yelling at, insulting, and berating employees of his various companies. Hilariously, Musk has called for a ban on abusive or cruel behaviour toward AI models, saying on his platform X that "cruelty to something that believes it is experiencing pain is not ok" Other leaders, including Steve Jobs, Gordon Ramsay and Martha Stewart have often been described as abusive, often having temper tantrums or other episodes at work where they displayed unwarranted levels of hostility toward subordinates. Several studies suggest that bullying by supervisors is a way to establish influence and status. This may help explain why lower-level supervisors abuse their subordinates. CEOs, however, already have plenty of influence and status, and it is unlikely that they engage in abusive supervision to get more. Research suggests that a personality trait, supervisors' social dominance orientation (SDO), is linked to abusive supervision.

stories.title: O'Toole revelling role in Ireland's 'Tom Squad'
stories.summary: It's hard to know where Tom O'Toole stood in Ireland's loosehead depth chart this time last year. The Ulster prop wasn't even in the Ireland squad last November, although he was on the fringes as part of the Ireland XV's team that defeated Spain in Madrid a year go. The main reason it's hard to pin where exactly he was in Ireland's loosehead standings is because at the time, he was very much a tighthead. A year previous Ireland had been flirting with the idea of making O'Toole a hybrid option; he came off the bench at loosehead against Fiji in November 2024, while he started there for Ireland A against England a few months later. Nothing really came of it until the start of 2026, when Andy Farrell saw his loosehead props drop like flies in the lead-up to the Six Nations, and O'Toole was drafted in to do a job on the left side of the scrum as a replacement against Italy. He has played every game for Ireland since; 10 matches in a row and five of those as a starter, and every one at loosehead.

stories.title: The split-second decisions & chance encounters that change lives
stories.summary: What links a Nobel laureate and a presidential chef to a Fanad farmer and a one-room school-teacher? A brand-new Irish book called Trace. Created by Donegal duo Laura Buchanan and Isla McGuckin, Trace brings together forty-eight contributors, from all walks of life, to share the split-second decisions, chance encounters, and twists of fate that have influenced their lives' paths. From the freedom of a first car to the ache of unrequited love, from opportunities missed to dreams boldly pursued, global adventurers, acclaimed artists and household names sit side-by-side with people who've forged fulfilling lives far closer to home. I was born in Belfast eight months before the end of the Second World War, when government rationing for food and clothing was in operation and would continue for another nine years. Ireland was a neutral country and its border with Northern Ireland became a smugglers' dream, where tea, sugar and butter found warmth up many a jumper. Money was in short supply as the world was coming to terms with the consequences of the war and the suffering inflicted upon nations. Countries scrambled to rebuild bombed buildings and infrastructure but fractured minds were more difficult to repair. There was little to celebrate in Belfast. I do have memories of street parties celebrating Queen Elizabeth II’s coronation. But there were no celebrations for St Patrick’s Day. Wearing a shamrock could lead to harassment and it was illegal to display the Irish flag. Still, my mother - who was an Irish nationalist from Presbyterian stock - insisted that we wear a shamrock lapel with tricoloured ribbons in our hair which unsettled some worshippers. Everything else just carried on as usual, except in nationalist areas where Catholic schools were closed and special masses were said - with the Our Father recited in Irish and the St Patrick’s hymn sung. Consequently, whilst I was aware of the celebrations worldwide, I had never actually taken part in any. But, in 1966, this was to change.

stories.title: Oti Mabuse gives birth to her second child
stories.summary: Dancing with the Stars Ireland head judge Oti Mabuse has announced she has given birth to her second child. The two-time Strictly Come Dancing champion, 36, has been married to Romanian dancer Marius Iepure since 2014. In June, Mabuse announced her pregnancy on Instagram, saying that "life had even bigger plans". Posting a photo in bed holding her son while her husband cuddled into her, Mabuse captioned her post: "We spent the whole weekend loving on our baby boy, taking turns holding him and saying 'just five more minutes' when it was time to hand him over. "Watching our little girl become a big sister has been one of the sweetest parts of it all. We keep looking at each other like, 'Can you believe this is our family?' All four of us together, and our hearts feel so full. We feel complete. "Welcome to the family, baby boy. Mummy, Daddy and your big sister love you so, so much. Oti & Marius x."

stories.title: Foldable phones: Apple iPhone Duo vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8
stories.summary: Journalist Glenn Kelly puts two foldable phones to the test*, comparing battery life, camera quality, design, dimensions, performance and price. Not so long ago, complaints ran rampant that the latest mobile phones just didn't cut the mustard. Perhaps they weren’t making the design revolutions buyers expected, or maybe they failed to improve battery life significantly. Either way, people were holding onto their devices for much longer than the standard two-year contract length. Well, 2026 has brought some good news for tech fans. Both Apple and Samsung have introduced devices that are getting people talking about - and dreaming of - owning a new handset once more...and this time it’s foldable. Today we are putting Apple’s first-ever foldable handset, the Duo, up against Samsung’s newest flexible friend, the Galaxy Z Fold 8. Can Apple win straight out of the gate? Or will Samsung’s experience win the day?

stories.title: Planning board set for new decision-making timelines
stories.summary: The Cabinet is expected to discuss significant changes to the planning system that are due to come into effect on Thursday. New decision-making timelines for An Coimisiún Pleanála as well as alterations to the planning judicial review process are being introduced as the Coalition seeks to expedite the planning process amid concerns over meeting its house-building targets. Minister for Housing James Browne and Minister of State for Planning John Cummins have a memo for Government outlining new consistent statutory decision-making timelines to be put in place for An Coimisiún Pleanála. Minor corrections to planning applications will also be facilitated to avoid the need for a whole new application process. There will also be provision made to provide for an alteration or modification of a planning permission alongside procedures for an extension to the duration of a planning permission. Changes to the application process for leave to bring judicial review proceedings on planning issues could deliver a time saving of around eight weeks.

stories.title: Battery EV surge continues to push Europe car sales
stories.summary: Rising demand for battery-operated electric vehicles continued to support growth in Europe's new-car market in October, offsetting another steep fall in petrol and diesel vehicle sales, data from the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) showed today. Demand for electrified vehicles remained strong across major European markets, supported by purchase incentives and a broader model lineup. New-car registrations, a proxy for sales, rose 3.4% year-on-year to 1.13 million vehicles across the European Union, Britain and the European Free Trade Association, ACEA said. Electrified cars accounted for 75.5% of all new vehicles registered in the euro zone in October. Petrol and diesel vehicle registrations fell 28.3% and 30.2%, respectively, now accounting for only 21.8% of new registrations. Registrations of battery-electric and plug-in hybrid cars jumped 56.1% and 9.2%, respectively, while hybrid car registrations fell 0.3%.

stories.title: Euro 2028 draw: Ireland's ideal and nightmare scenarios

The likelihood, as manager Heimir Hallgrimsson pointed out in the post-match press conference after beating Kosovo, is that Ireland will be in a four-team group given their involvement in the UEFA Nations League play-offs. In the less likely scenario that they are in a five-team group, the pot one team they would face would be Italy or Greece because a five-team group could only contain a maximum of one side involved in Nations League finals or play-offs, which does not apply to the two aforementioned countries. stories.title: Ted Lasso renewed for fifth series
stories.summary: Ted Lasso has been renewed for a fifth series by Apple TV, with Jason Sudeikis set to return as the star and executive producer. The US actor plays the title character, an American football coach who is hired to manage fictional English football club AFC Richmond despite having no experience in the sport. The hit comedy, which also stars Brett Goldstein, Nick Mohammed and Hannah Waddingham. first hit screens in 2020 and went on to earn the most Emmy nominations ever received by a first-season comedy. Its third series appeared to bring the show to a conclusion as Lasso returned to America after AFC Richmond narrowly missed out on the Premier League title. However, the comedy returned for a fourth series in August, with Lasso lured back to the UK to manage Richmond's women’s team. The latest instalment welcomed Sex Education star Tanya Reynolds as Alice Chilton, alongside newcomers Abbie Hern, Aisling Sharkey, Rex Hayes, Faye Marsay and Jude Mack.

stories.title: Nuala Carey: "I'm actually quite a lucky person"
stories.summary: Weather presenter Nuala Carey is a naturally upbeat person, even when telling us about days of dismal downpours. She talks to Claire O'Mahony about bidding farewell to the weekly Lotto draws, the joy of judging the Rose of Tralee and how she incorporates exercise into her family routine. If you want to know what Irish people really worry about when it comes to the weather, just ask Nuala Carey. "People are more in the present," she explains. "They want to talk about the weather that we have at the moment or what might be coming next week." Interestingly, it’s children who are more likely to bring up climate change, something Nuala has noticed during visits to schools. "They talk more about climate change, but that’s because they’re learning all of that at school and it would be fresh on their minds," she says, praising the work schools do around recycling and their Green Flag programmes. Hundreds of photographs arrive throughout the year and choosing which ones make the final selection – a job that Nuala shares with a panel of judges – isn’t always straightforward. "We like to have a spread, if we can, of counties. And it is the weather photo calendar, so we do like to show different types of weather," she explains. "In Ireland, you can get four seasons in one day, never mind in the year." For the amateur photographers, there’s also the thrill of seeing their work on television, as Nuala and the weather team feature them in their forecasts, and the possibility of having their work displayed in people’s homes for an entire month.

stories.title: Govt to consider use of plug-in solar panels from April
stories.summary: Householders could be permitted to buy and use plug-in solar panels from next Spring under new energy affordability measures to be discussed by Cabinet later today. Minister for Climate, Environment and Energy Darragh O'Brien will brief his ministerial colleagues on the Coalition's latest attempts to drive down energy costs for consumers and businesses amid consistent opposition criticism of the Government's efforts to tackle spiralling energy bills. It is currently illegal to buy plug-in solar panels, but Mr O'Brien will tell Cabinet how a new expert review advises the devices could be rolled out across Ireland from next April. The panels can be plugged into a standard wall socket to generate solar power from a balcony, shed roof or any other outdoor space. The devices cost in the region of €500 but could save households between €130 and €150 a year as they generally provide up to 20% of an average home's electricity use. Larger-scale systems can last between 20 and 25 years. In May, Mr O'Brien tasked officials at the ESB, National Standards Authority of Ireland, Safe Electric and the Commission for the Regulation of Utilities to examine how to permit the use of plug-in solar systems in Ireland, an energy measure popular in other European countries as well as in Britain.

stories.title: Kingfisher edges up full year profit outlook
stories.summary: European home improvement retailer Kingfisher has edged-up its full-year profit outlook after it reported a 0.8% rise in third quarter underlying like-for-like sales with a robust performance in the UK and Poland offsetting weakness in France. The FTSE-100 listed group owns B&Q and Screwfix in Ireland and the UK and Castorama and Brico Depot in France and other markets. It said its total group sales in the third quarter to October 31 rose 1.5% on a constant currency basis to £3.26 billion. Kingfisher said its performance was led by Screwfix, Poland and Iberia and underpinned by solid broad-based core category performance. "We delivered a solid quarter, with continued market share gains and strong momentum across our strategic growth drivers of trade, e-commerce and marketplace," CEO Thierry Garnier said. Like-for-like sales increased 2.4% in the UK & Ireland and were up 2.1% in Poland and 6.6% in Iberia but were down 2.8% in France.

stories.title: Ireland's rediscovered identity key to their resurgence
stories.summary: Ireland's victory over South Africa and their performances throughout the Nations Championship have been marked by the return of a distinct identity to their playing strategy. Everything communicated from the Irish camp over the past number of weeks suggests that a new line has been drawn. Ireland's coaching staff have conducted a review of their own processes and what they want from the team going forward. The outcome appears to be an even greater expectation of the players, alongside an improvement in fitness levels to allow Ireland to play with increased tempo and intensity. While other teams around the world can select bigger and more powerful players, Ireland will always struggle to compete on those terms. It is not that Andy Farrell couldn't select a bigger pack, but Ireland will never match the sheer size of the South African or French forward units. Ireland have had to cut their cloth accordingly. They cannot simply add meaningful size to their existing players, and even if they wanted to prioritise selecting a few bigger bodies, a couple of injuries could quickly derail that approach. Quite simply, Ireland do not have the same depth of players in that physical category. What the coaches and players can influence, however, is their strategy, skill levels, ability to identify space and execution of the game plan. Their attacking approach from setpiece has been particularly evident throughout November. There have been intricate plays designed to move the ball into wider channels, creating opportunities for the outside backs to attack the defensive line with time and space.

stories.title: Recruitment campaign begins for Census 2027 roles
stories.summary: A nationwide recruitment campaign for 3,850 Field Support Officers to help deliver Census 2027 is now under way, with €3,000 on offer for part-time work over eight weeks. The officers, who will replace the traditional Census Enumerators, will support households in understanding how, where and when they can complete their census form. For the first time, households will also have the option to fill out the census online. Applications for the role opened this morning and will remain so until Friday 4 December at 2pm. However, the Central Statistics Office (CSO) has advised those interested to apply early, as the window will close when 12,000 applications have been received. Officers will be responsible for between 450 to 850 houses and are set to go door-to-door between 5 April and 9 May next year.

stories.title: St Eunan's seek answers on disputed Scotstown equaliser
stories.summary: St Eunan's have called on the relevant authorities to examine the circumstances surrounding the controversial point that they believe denied them victory in Saturday’s Ulster Senior Club Championship semi-final against Scotstown. The Letterkenny club are seeking clarification after a late free from Kieran Hughes was awarded as a point, despite the ball appearing to sail wide of the posts. The decision came at the end of extra time at Brewster Park, with referee Kieran Eannetta consulting his umpires before allowing the score to stand. The point brought the teams level at 1-24 to 0-27 and sent the contest to a penalty shoot-out, where the reigning provincial champions prevailed 4-2 to book their place in the Ulster final against Crossmaglen Rangers. In a statement issued on Monday evening, St Eunan’s outlined their disappointment and said the incident had left players, management and supporters with a strong feeling of injustice. "St Eunan’s GAA Club wishes to express its profound disappointment following Saturday evening’s Ulster Senior Club Championship semi-final against Scotstown," the statement from the club reads.

stories.title: Two Irish authors on first Children's Booker shortlist
stories.summary: Two Irish authors have been shortlisted for the inaugural Children's Booker Prize, as eight books compete for the £50,000 award. The prestigious prize, unveiled last year, will recognise the best contemporary fiction for children aged eight to 12 published in the UK or Ireland, either originally written in English or translated from other languages. The shortlist was selected from 89 submissions and features five novels, two graphic novels and an illustrated collection of short stories. Irish author Eoin Colfer is nominated for 'War', along with British co-author Andrew Donkin. Illustrated by Giovanni Rigano, 'War' follows a 14-year-old graffiti artist navigating an invasion in an unnamed European city. Séamus Almost Famous by Jessica Scott-Whyte, illustrated by Becka Moor, follows a young Irish boy determined to find fame after discovering he is the only member of his family without it. She explained that her book tells the story of a young Co Kilkenny boy, Séamus, who is the only person in his family who is not famous and how he sets about changing that.

stories.title: Ireland have 'a full squad of fit bodies' for Wallabies
stories.summary: While head coach Andy Farrell will be sweating on the availability of his captain Dan Sheehan for this week's final Nations Championship outing, the Ireland head coach has no new injuries to contend with ahead of the meeting with Australia in London on Friday. The IRFU are yet to receive details on when Sheehan will face a disciplinary hearing after the yellow card he picked up in Saturday's win against South Africa was upgraded to a red. Sheehan was initially shown yellow for a croc-roll on Marco van Staden eight minutes from time in the 20-17 victory, before confirmation it would become a red card after being assessed by the game's foul play review officer. With a six-day turnaround between the win against the Springboks and Friday's meeting with the Wallabies, the Ireland squad have already got back down to work for their final game of the Nations Championship, with their game against Australia set to decide fifth and sixth place in the inaugural competition. And despite "a few sore bodies", Farrell appears to be playing with a full deck when he names his matchday squad on Wednesday afternoon. "That was a physical affair, as we knew it was going to be," assistant coach Andrew Goodman (below) said of Saturday's win.

stories.title: Trump orders federal executions to be expedited
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump has ordered that federal executions be expedited at an event condemning California Governor Gavin Newsom's decision to commute all death sentences in his state. Mr Newsom, who is widely expected to make a run for the White House in 2028, announced the decision to change the sentences of the state's more than 500 death row inmates to life in prison earlier this month. Mr Trump took aim at the move during an event at the Department of Justice in which multiple relatives of victims spoke in opposition to Mr Newsom's decision. "We come together to stand against the travesty and to wrap our arms around the families of victims who were so brutally betrayed by bad government and our political system," Mr Trump said, calling Mr Newsom a "terrible" governor. Mr Trump was joined by Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel at the event, which featured families of murder victims. "Mr President, I assure you that this Department of Justice is seeking the death penalty whenever appropriate for crimes committed in this country," Mr Blanche said while introducing him, adding that the Justice Department has sought the death penalty 49 times since the ‌start of the administration.

stories.title: Classy Brentford put 10-man Everton to the sword
stories.summary: Vitaly Janelt scored a 30-yard screamer as Brentford romped to a 4-0 victory against 10-man Everton at the Gtech Community Stadium. One win in five had seen some of the early season optimism around Keith Andrews' team fade but this was an emphatic response to fire them up the Premier League table to sixth, even if culpability for Everton’s collapse lay largely with James Tarkowski, red carded in the 40th minute for a horror tackle on Yehor Yarmolyuk. David Moyes was setting a new record for number of games in charge, this his 593rd match eclipsing the tally of Harry Catterick racked up during the 60s and 70s, but this was a terrible first half and was no way to mark such an achievement. Everything went wrong for the visitors. Both Brentford goals scored by Keane Lewis-Potter came via deflections and Tarkowski’s momentary abdication of responsibility as captain, lunging studs-up into the shin of Yarmolyuk with his team 2-0 down, would have been impossible for Moyes to mitigate. He was let down badly by one of his senior players in a moment of direst need. Thereafter the game was little contest. It might have trickled towards a routine two-goal win for Brentford had Janelt not pulled out a brilliant strike from range that ripped past Jordan Pickford to rub salt in the wound for Moyes, and for Tarkowski. Fabio Carvalho bundled one in from on the goal-line with his knee in stoppage time, the final indignity for Everton.

stories.title: Five women killed every hour by relatives in 2025 - UN
stories.summary: More than 47,000 women and girls, or around five per hour, were killed by relatives around the world in 2025, a figure broadly unchanged from previous years, according to a UN report published today. The number of women and girls killed by an intimate partner or a family member has fluctuated between 45,000 and 51,000 over the past several years, according to estimates by UN Women and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime. Of the 78,000 women and girls who were victims of intentional homicide last year, around 60% were killed by an intimate partner or family member, the report said ahead of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women. The estimated 47,000 victims represent 129 women and girls killed every day. The figure was calculated using an analysis of statistics from 122 countries and territories. While women accounted for 19% of homicide victims worldwide in 2025, 60% of them were killed in the private sphere. By contrast, 11% of male homicide victims were killed in such circumstances. The UN stressed the "urgency of ensuring that the prevention of domestic violence addresses intimate relationships, as well as relationships in wider family structures".

stories.title: Cttee to meet for extra day to hasten Triple Lock debate
stories.summary: The Oireachtas Committee on Defence will meet for an extra day this week in a bid to speed up its discussions over the potential Triple Lock law change. Its understood the committee will now meet on Wednesday between 6pm and 9pm, in addition to Tuesday evening and Thursday morning sessions. The decision was taken due to the fact 224 amendments have been submitted for examination by the committee - a figure likely to take a significant amount of time to go through in detail. While the committee has a one-person Government majority, there is a widespread belief Opposition committee members will seek to slow walk the amendments discussed, a possible move Opposition parties say is about closely examining all amendments. Although the Government can in theory guillotine discussions due to its majority, there is a similar belief this would be seen as limiting debate. Minister for Defence Helen McEntee, Taoiseach Micheál Martin and Tánaiste Simon Harris among others have stressed in recent weeks that they want the Triple Lock to be removed and the Defence Amendment Bill signed into law by the end of the year.

stories.summary: Decorated midfielder Gary O'Neill has joined Waterford FC from Shamrock Rovers on a season-long loan. The 31-year old from Tralee won six Premier Division titles and two FAI Cup medals since joining the Hoops from UCD. He returned to action late on this season after receiving an all-clear. In his first season in 2019, O'Neill scored the winning penalty in the FAI Cup final as Shamrock Rovers ended a 32-year famine in the competition. He racked up over 200 appearances for the Tallaght club as they established domination in the league in the 2020s, winning four titles in a row between 2020 and 2023. "I’m very proud in all honesty - obviously over the last couple of years I’ve had a difficult time, but I’ve gotten myself back to a really good place.

"I’m incredibly proud of what we’ve achieved together so far, but what excites me most is what lies ahead. "For now, all our attention turns to Poland. We know what's at stake, we know what this opportunity means to everyone, and no question we’ll give absolutely everything we have to make the country proud."

stories.title: Rejoining EU without referendum 'unthinkable' - Burnham
stories.summary: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said that rejoining the European Union without a referendum would be "unthinkable", as he accused predecessors warning him against reigniting the Brexit debate of being "stuck in the past". Mr Burnham has in recent weeks smashed a consensus that Britain's acrimonious departure from the European Union was done and dusted, floating the possibility that Britain could apply to rejoin. Britain narrowly voted to leave the 27-member bloc in 2016. Now, pro-Brexit voices are reorganising to prepare for likely looming battles as Mr Burnham vows to lay out options for Britain's long-term relationship with the EU. Asked in parliament whether he would give a "clear and unequivocal" statement that taking Britain back into the EU without a referendum would be "unthinkable", Mr Burnham replied: "Yes it would be unthinkable." In recent days, former Conservative prime ministers Rishi Sunak, Theresa May, David Cameron and Boris Johnson have all urged Labour leader Mr Burnham not to reopen old wounds. "Those who say we shouldn't talk about Brexit risk leaving Britain stuck in the past with a substandard set of arrangements," Mr Burnham told parliament.

stories.title: Man with Alzheimer's found alive after 11 days in Amazon
stories.summary: A 74-year-old man with Alzheimer's disease was found alive after 11 days lost in Brazil's Amazon rainforest, where he ate wild fruit and slept on beds of leaves, rescuers and local media reports said. Nine days later, his granddaughter Sara Montes urged firefighters to keep looking for him. In a video posted on Instagram, she said they planned to suspend the search on Sunday. "Don't forget about us. Don't forget about Grandpa," she pleaded. Rescuers found him Friday about 10km from where he disappeared, according to social media posts by a group of park rangers and one of the rescuers. Images from the rescue show him sitting in his underwear, looking disoriented.
